lines: SDD moves cost to planning rather than removing it. One Reddit team measured spec-driven runs at two to three times the tokens, and about twice the wall-clock time, of direct prompting. One participant complained that eighty percent of tokens went into making a plan. The savings people reported were rework avoided, not a smaller bill.
Split. Tool users found long, agent-written specs hard to read, and human attention became the bottleneck. Some tool makers found that reviewing a concise spec was easier than reviewing code.
Talk about drift. This is the part I'd want every engineering lead to internalize.

The paper separates two failure modes. Implementation drift is when the agent departs from the spec while building. Spec decay is when the spec goes stale as later changes alter the code. Their example: the spec says sessions expire after thirty minutes. If the agent builds sixty, that's drift. If a later change sets sixty on purpose, and the spec still says thirty, that's decay.

Right. People who saw drift tightened their instructions, making conventions explicit in instruction files. People who saw decay limited their specs or linked them together. And here's the key point. An automated check can tell you that spec and code disagree. It can't tell you which one is wrong. A person has to decide.
Which runs straight into finding eleven.
Evaluation effort grows with the system, and it outgrows human review. One participant said of a thousand-line agent change, I'm not reading it.

Adoption inertia. Individuals who introduced SDD to their teams usually met resistance. One said it worked for them personally, but the whole team has to switch. Another wanted more research, because people don't believe experience.
